rss.text_excerpt:
November 3, 2026 — A quiet day lets us share some behind the senes. There’s a lot of dispute to yesterday’s title story on “ Weight Space Programming ” — and we agree that some of the claims are presented in overly favorable light and overall took away from the impact of the paper’s more substantial discoveries. However it is still a big wakeup moment and has had multiple independent replications by now that it is not worth either doing some kind of retraction or a followup title story saying it was bogus. Weight-Space Programming: Frontier Models Reading and Writing Neural Network Weights Core claim and replications : Several groups report that frontier LLMs can generate or edit small networks' weights directly, without gradient training or tools. Cross-generation replication : Alex Krentsel's replication of MIT's experiment found a sharp capability jump across model generations; the latest models generated Breakout networks scoring up to 22× an RL-trained baseline ( summary ). Hugging Face reproduction : Hugging Face reproduced the paper with ML Intern, its open-source AI-research harness, and released the model and a demo ( NielsRogge ). Hand-written classifier : A user had Fable hand-write a 100K-parameter network that classifies real versus fake legal citations, reportedly outperforming a trained version ( jacsebl ). Legora's CTO highlighted the result ( mstockton ). Astra's Qwen edit, reconstructed : GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 weights in Qwen3.5-0.8B without backprop, raising MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%. A Zhihu reconstruction from the logs shows the gain is narrower than the headline ( ZhihuFrontier ): Failure mode : 576 of 579 repaired answers had originally hit the 32K-token limit because of looping. Method : Astra derived a "repetition direction" from contrastive looping/productive contexts, located it mainly in the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted 6× the projection from the top 64 aligned neurons per layer. Held-out result : Accuracy rose from 10.6% to 60.4% on 1,152 held-out problems. Most of the gain is existing reasoning that can now finish. Laptop reproduction : Simon Willison reports that Qwen 3.8 27B achieved the same weight-interpretation feat on his laptop after 45+ minutes ( simonw ). rss.title: A thousand fewer paths to root
rss.summary: OpenAI built an autonomous pipeline that found, validated, and generated patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel.
rss.text_excerpt:
Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area. Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access. We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches. In June, as part of our Patch the Planet initiative , we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches. Summary At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results. The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes. In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. rss.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
rss.summary: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally". The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. rss.title: How Cisco defends at machine speed with OpenAI
rss.summary: Cisco combines network intelligence with OpenAI models to strengthen enterprise security. Learn how it is building more adaptive defenses.
rss.text_excerpt:
Cisco builds the networking and security infrastructure that organizations rely on to connect and protect their systems. As adversaries leverage AI to scale automated attacks and craft exploits at machine-speed, defending enterprise infrastructure must evolve. Pairing Cisco’s vast network telemetry with frontier AI reasoning gives defenders the toolkit necessary to outpace emerging threats. OpenAI’s rigorous approach to enterprise data privacy—centered on zero data retention, strict customer data boundaries, and verifiable isolation—means Cisco could confidently deploy frontier intelligence across mission-critical systems without compromising customer priorities or sensitive telemetry. Cisco’s defense starts where threats move: the network. In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. rss.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
rss.summary: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here's a link to the larger image . For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. TensorFold enables automatic public check-ins: a successful new claim starts an anonymous session on the radar and returns its `session` number. Keep that number instead of starting a duplicate session. For work already yours, start a session with `atc start ISSUE --json`. github.text_excerpt: # VibeSys: Generating Bespoke Systems with AI Agents [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2605.06068-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06068) **An agentic framework that generates bespoke systems from application requirements, workload characteristics, and the underlying hardware.** ## News - **2026-11-04** — [VibeSys on Trainium](https://syfi.cs.washington.edu/blog/2026-11-04-vibesys-trainium/): agents build and tune Qwen3.8 serving engines on AWS Trainium2. - **2026-10-08** — [VibeSys on AMD MI300A](https://syfi.cs.washington.edu/blog/2026-10-08-qwen35-mi300a/): an agent-built Qwen3.5-397B engine achieves 2.3× the goodput of tuned SGLang. - **2026-05-12** — [Introducing VibeServe](https://syfi.cs.washington.edu/blog/2026-05-12-introducing-vibeserve/): let AI agents write your serving stack. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06068). ## About VibeSys Today's systems software is built for generality. A serving engine, operating system, or database supports many workloads and hardware platforms, but its shared abstractions can leave opportunities in any one deployment unexploited. Specialization can recover large gains; building and maintaining a separate system for each deployment has rarely justified the engineering cost. Coding agents are beginning to change that calculation. **VibeSys uses AI agents to build and optimize bespoke systems for a specific application, workload, and hardware target.** You provide the requirements, correctness checks, and performance benchmark. Agents explore system designs, implement candidates, and use measurements to guide the next change. Persistent search history and independent review let that process continue across many experiments, while domain skills supply the knowledge needed for serving engines, databases, microservices, and kernels. VibeSys can start from an existing codebase or build a system from scratch. [**VibeServe**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06068) demonstrated this approach for LLM serving: agents generated complete serving systems that exploit deployment knowledge across scheduling, memory management, and kernels. On predicted-output code editing, a generated system achieved up to **5.95× the speed of vLLM's standard decoding**. VibeSys extends this approach to systems software more broadly, with each task defining what must remain correct and what to optimize.

# Kolega Code **A terminal coding agent where the model writes its own multi-agent workflows.** [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/kolega-code)](https://pypi.org/project/kolega-code/) [![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/kolega-code)](https://pypi.org/project/kolega-code/) [![CI](https://github.com/kolega-ai/kolega-code/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/kolega-ai/kolega-code/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Coverage](docs/src/assets/coverage.svg)](https://github.com/kolega-ai/kolega-code/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-kolega--ai.github.io-blue)](https://kolega-ai.github.io/kolega-code/) [![Changelog](https://img.shields.io/badge/changelog-keep%20up-blue)](CHANGELOG.md) Kolega Code is a local-first terminal coding agent. For work that is too broad for one agent loop, its **Gigacode** engine has the model write a Python program that orchestrates multiple sub-agents. The runtime then executes that program. ![Kolega Code in action](docs/src/assets/demo.gif) ## Gigacode: model-authored orchestration For a repo-wide review, a migration, or a plan with independent workstreams, the model writes an orchestration program instead of delegating workers one at a time. The program can combine parallel phases, pipelines, adversarial verification, judge panels, and synthesis gates to fit the task. The runtime saves the script so it can be inspected and run again. Claude Code uses the same model-authored approach for its dynamic workflows (ultracode). Kolega Code provides an open, provider-agnostic implementation whose runtime source is available in this repository. The runtime journals each completed agent call to disk. Resume is content-keyed rather than positional: when you use `resume_from_run_id`, calls with unchanged semantic inputs replay from the journal at zero token cost. This still works if the script was edited or reordered, and it works across sessions and process restarts. Read [how gigacode works](how-gigacode-works.md) for the architecture, or an [unedited model-authored workflow](examples/parallel-code-review.py) with its full provenance and execution record. ## How it works The model investigates your repo, then writes a Python program against a small runtime API (`agent`, `parallel`, `pipeline`, `phase`, `budget`). **English** | [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) | [日本語](README.ja.md) # Abyss: Non-invasive observability platform for AI Agent

## Overview Abyss is an open-source observability platform for AI agents. It observes agent-to-provider network traffic through a local proxy, helping developers and teams understand conversations, tool activity, token usage, and network failures without modifying agent source code or adding instrumentation to agent applications. Built in Rust, Abyss provides: - Explicit HTTP/HTTPS proxying and transparent proxying through macOS Network Extension and Windows WFP adapters. - Policy-controlled TLS interception and content capture for supported agent protocols. - Normalized events for model API protocols, including OpenAI's Responses API and Chat Completions API, and Anthropic's Messages API. - Plugins and Rust, TypeScript, and Python SDKs for custom integrations and event delivery. ## Install Install the prebuilt CLI on Linux x86_64 (with systemd) or macOS ARM64: ```bash curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL \ https://github.com/lexmount/abyss-rs/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh ``` ## Quick Start With Node.js 22+ and npm 10+ installed, start the local environment and run an installed agent through Abyss: ```bash abyss deploy-local start abyss run -- codex ``` Open the Abyss dashboard to explore sessions, model activity, and token usage: ```bash abyss dashboard ``` See the [Abyss CLI guide](https://abyss.lexmount.com/docs/product/open-source-software/abyss-cli) for configuration, capture controls, and lifecycle commands. ## Supported Harnesses and Models | Harnesses | Desktop | CLI | Web | | --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | | ChatGPT | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | |
